professional-requests.title: Write the request
professional-requests.brief: You need the invoice numbers from Tomás in Finance. You need them today.
professional-requests.task: Write a short email to Tomás. Say hello, ask politely, give a time, and say thank you.

checks.label: Does not use 'until' for a deadline

selfCheck: Is my request polite?
Does Tomás know when I need it?
Is there only one request?
professional-requests.model:
Hi Tomás,

Could you please send me the invoice numbers for June by 4 p.m. today? I need them for Elena's report this evening.

If you have any questions, please call me.

Thanks for your help,
Ana

deadline-language.title: Move the deadline
deadline-language.brief: Your report is for Friday, but the supplier sent the data late. You can finish it by Tuesday. You are in the office until 6 p.m. today.
deadline-language.task: Write a short email to your manager. Say the report will be late, why, and the new day. Use 'by' and 'until' correctly.
include: The problem: the report will be late
When you are free today, with 'until'

checks.label: Does not use 'until' for the deadline

selfCheck: Did I use 'by' for the new deadline?
Did I use 'until' only for time that continues?
deadline-language.model:
Hi Elena,

I'm sorry, but the report will be late. The supplier sent the data three days late.

I can send you the report by Tuesday at 12.

I'm in the office until 6 p.m. today if you want to talk.

Thanks,
Ana

apologising.title: Write the apology
apologising.brief: Yesterday you sent a client, Ms Lemoine, the wrong report. She wrote to tell you.
apologising.task: Write a short reply. Say sorry once, send the right report, and say what you will do next time.
include: The correct report (say it is attached)
What you will do next time

checks.label: Says what you will do next time

selfCheck: Did I say sorry only once?
Is the correct report attached?
Is my email short and clear?
apologising.model:
Dear Ms Lemoine,

Thank you for your email. I'm sorry, I sent you the wrong report yesterday. That was my mistake.

Please find the correct report attached. From now on, I will check every file before I send it.

Kind regards,
Ana Ruiz

polite-disagreement.title: Disagree out loud
polite-disagreement.brief: In a team meeting your manager says the new onboarding flow is not worth the development time, and wants to park it. You disagree, and you have data: forty per cent of new users drop out at step three.
polite-disagreement.task: Disagree with your manager, in front of the team, without damaging the relationship.
checklist: I acknowledged their concern before disagreeing
I named one specific concern rather than rejecting everything
I used a number or a piece of evidence
I proposed something concrete rather than only objecting
I spoke about the idea, not about the person
I did not say 'I am not agree'
polite-disagreement.model: I see the concern about development time, and I know the roadmap is full. Can I share one number before we park it? Forty per cent of new users drop out at step three, which is where the flow breaks. If we fix just that step, the build pays for itself in about two months. So rather than parking the whole thing, could we scope a smaller version that only touches step three, and come back to the rest next quarter?

giving-opinions.title: Give your opinion
giving-opinions.brief: Your team is talking about a new idea: no meetings on Fridays. Your manager asks you: 'What do you think?'
giving-opinions.task: Give your opinion, a reason, and a small example. About 30 seconds.
checklist: I started with 'I think…' or 'In my opinion…'
I gave a clear answer (yes or no)
I gave a reason with 'because'
I gave a small example
I did not say 'according to me'
giving-opinions.model: In my opinion, it's a good idea. I think we have too many meetings, because every day I have three or four. For example, last Friday I had no time to finish my report. With no meetings on Fridays, I can finish my work before the weekend.

suggestions-advice.title: Suggest an idea
suggestions-advice.brief: Your colleague Leo has a problem. The team meeting is always too long, and nobody decides anything. He asks you for ideas.
suggestions-advice.task: Write a short reply. Make one suggestion for the team and give Leo one piece of advice.
include: A suggestion with 'How about…?' or 'Why don't we…?'
selfCheck: Is my suggestion easy to try?
Did I use the base verb after 'should'?
suggestions-advice.model:
Hi Leo,

How about having a shorter meeting, only 30 minutes? We could also send the agenda the day before.

You should talk to Elena about it, because she wants shorter meetings too.

Good luck!
Ana

clarifying.title: Ask a clear question
clarifying.brief: Your manager, Elena, writes: 'Can you prepare something short on the sales numbers for Thursday?' You don't know if she wants a document or slides.
clarifying.task: Write a short reply. Say yes, ask one clear question with two choices, and say when it will be ready.
include: One question with two choices ('… or …?')

checks.label: Asks a question with two choices
Says when it will be ready

selfCheck: Can my manager answer in one word?
Is my question polite?
clarifying.model:
Hi Elena,

Yes, of course. Quick question: do you want a one-page document or some slides?

I can have it ready on Wednesday afternoon, so you have time to read it before Thursday.

Thanks,
Ana

email-structure.title: Write the holiday email
email-structure.brief: You are on holiday next week, from Monday to Friday. Daniel will do your work. There is a client call on Thursday at 10 a.m.
email-structure.task: Write a short email to Daniel. Give the dates, the one important task, and where your notes are.
include: The client call: day and time
selfCheck: Can Daniel do the work with only this email?
Is the day and time of the call clear?
Did I start with a greeting and finish with a closing?
email-structure.model:
Hi Daniel,

I'm on holiday next week, from Monday 6th to Friday 10th. Thank you for doing my work.

There is one important thing: the client call on Thursday at 10 a.m.

All my notes are in the shared folder.

Best regards,
Ana

async-writing.title: Write the async update
async-writing.brief: Your team lead is eight hours behind you and will read this when she wakes up. You finished the API integration yesterday and started the migration script today, but you are blocked: you need staging credentials from Marc in Infra.
async-writing.task: Write the daily update so she can act on it without replying to ask you anything.
include: What is blocking you, and who can unblock it
A time, in a way that survives the time difference

checks.label: Does not open with a bare greeting

selfCheck: Could she act on this before I wake up?
Is the blocker impossible to miss?
Did I avoid making her ask a follow-up question?
async-writing.model:
Yesterday: finished the API integration, all tests passing.
Today: starting the migration script.
Blocked on: staging credentials from Infra.

@Marc could you drop those in the channel when you're on? It blocks me from about 11:00 my time, so if it lands before your end of day I won't lose a run.

Everything else is on track for Thursday.

professional-tone.title: Rewrite the cold message
professional-tone.brief: You sent a colleague this message: 'This isn't what I asked for.' She replied 'Ok.' and has gone quiet. What you actually need is the regional split rather than the totals, and you still need it by tomorrow at noon because it goes to the board.
professional-tone.task: Write the repair message. Own the tone without over-apologising, supply the information you left out, keep the deadline firm, and offer time.
include: Acknowledge how the message landed, in one sentence
Say specifically what you need instead, and why
Keep the deadline firm without sounding curt
Offer to go through it together
selfCheck: Would I be relieved to receive this?
Did I supply the missing information, not just the apology?
Is the deadline still clear without sounding like an order?
professional-tone.model:
Hi Nadia,

Sorry, that came out sharper than I meant it. What I actually need is the regional split rather than the totals, because the board wants to see where the drop came from, and I should have said so the first time.

It still needs to be with me by noon tomorrow, as it goes into the board pack that afternoon. Are you free at three today? Happy to go through it together so you're not second-guessing what I'm after.

Ana

softening.title: Raise the error safely
softening.brief: A senior colleague's report has a figure in the second column that does not match the appendix. You are fairly sure it is wrong, but not certain. You are commenting on the shared document.
softening.task: Write the comment. Challenge the number without accusing anyone, and leave room to be wrong yourself.
include: The exact location of the problem
selfCheck: Is there exactly one hedge?
Could they fix it from my comment alone?
Does it attack the document rather than the person?
softening.model: I might be missing something here, but the figure in the second column looks different from the appendix total on page 9. Is the column meant to include returns? Happy to be corrected if I've read it wrong.

saying-no.title: Say no, properly
saying-no.brief: A colleague has asked you to review a forty-page document by tomorrow. You are already at capacity, and saying yes means something else slips.
saying-no.task: Write the reply. Refuse clearly, but offer something real.
include: A genuine partial offer or an alternative date
A question handing the choice back
selfCheck: Is my no unambiguous?
Is what I offered genuinely deliverable?
Did I protect the relationship as well as my week?
saying-no.model:
I can't get through all forty pages by tomorrow, I'm afraid — I've got the Ortiz review landing the same day.

What I can do tonight is read the executive summary and the recommendations properly, which is usually where the risk sits. Would that help, or do you need the full read? If it's the full read, I could do it by Tuesday morning.

meeting-language.title: Close the meeting
meeting-language.brief: Five minutes are left. Three things were decided: supplier B, the launch moves to 14 April, and Ana owns the content plan. Two things are still open: the budget for an extra designer, and who presents to the board.
meeting-language.task: Close the meeting out loud. Summarise the decisions, name the owners, and say what is still open.
checklist: I signalled the summary ('to summarise', 'so, to recap')
I listed all three decisions
I named who owns what
I said explicitly what is still unresolved
I put a deadline on the open items
I did not just say 'great discussion everyone'
meeting-language.model: So, to summarise: we're going with supplier B, the launch moves to 14 April, and Ana owns the content plan. On actions, Ana sends the first draft on Tuesday, I'll review it by Thursday, and we confirm on Friday. Still open: the budget for the extra designer, and who presents to the board. Can we close both of those by Friday? I'll put fifteen minutes in on Thursday if that's easier than doing it over email.

explaining-problems.title: Explain what went wrong
explaining-problems.brief: Integration testing has found a data problem affecting about a third of the records. The launch moves from 1 April to mid-April. You have two people on the clean-up and have asked the vendor for support. You need the sponsor to decide: hold the date and cut scope, or move the date.
explaining-problems.task: Explain it to the project sponsor. You have about a minute.
checklist: I said what happened before anything else
I gave the impact in dates or numbers
I said what I have already done
I ended with the specific decision I need
I did not open with an excuse
I did not overstate it
explaining-problems.model: Integration testing has found a data problem we hadn't seen. It affects about a third of the records. The impact is that the launch moves roughly two weeks, so mid-April rather than the 1st. I've already got two people on the clean-up and I've asked the vendor for support, and I'll have a firm date from them by Thursday. What I need from you is a decision: either we hold the original date and cut the reporting module from the first release, or we move the date and ship it complete. My recommendation is to move it, but it's your call on the launch commitment.

feedback.title: Give the difficult feedback
feedback.brief: A junior colleague, Iris, has sent you a draft with three factual errors: the Q2 figure on page 2, the client name in the header, and the date in the summary. It has to go out today.
feedback.task: Write the feedback. Make it specific enough to act on and kind enough to keep her confidence.

checks.label: Counts them so they feel finite

selfCheck: Is every correction locatable?
Did I comment on the work rather than on Iris?
Would she know exactly what to do in the next ten minutes?
feedback.model:
Thanks Iris — the structure works well, and the decision table on page 4 is much clearer than the last version.

Three things need correcting before it goes out: the Q2 figure on page 2 doesn't match the appendix, the client name in the header is still the old one, and the date in the summary says March rather than April.

Could you turn those around by two? Then it can go out this afternoon.

negotiating.title: Write the counter-offer
negotiating.brief: You have been offered 48k. Your researched range was 52 to 58k. The role itself is genuinely good and you want it.
negotiating.task: Write the reply. Keep the offer alive, counter clearly, and give them a second route if the cash is fixed.
include: A justification that is about the role, not your costs
An alternative if the budget cannot move

checks.label: Justifies by the role, not personal costs
Offers a second currency if cash is fixed

selfCheck: Would they still want to hire me after reading this?
Is my figure attached to a reason about the job?
Have I given them a way to say yes even if cash is fixed?
negotiating.model:
Thank you — I'm genuinely pleased, and I'd very much like to take the role.

On the figure: 48 is a little below where I'd hoped. Given the scope, particularly owning the client reporting from day one, I was looking at around 54. Is there flexibility to get there?

If the budget is fixed at 48, could we look at a formal review at six months instead, or at the training budget? I'd be happy with either route.

comparing.title: Write the recommendation
comparing.brief: Two suppliers. Vidal is about 15% more expensive but delivers in four weeks. Orsan is cheaper but takes eight weeks. The launch date is fixed.
comparing.task: Write a short recommendation to the budget holder. Compare the two, quantify the trade-off, and commit to one.
include: The trade-off, with numbers on both sides
A clear recommendation, not a summary of options
The reason your recommendation wins given the fixed launch date

checks.label: Links it to the launch date

selfCheck: Did I actually recommend one, or just describe both?
Are both sides of the trade-off quantified?
Could the budget holder decide from this alone?
comparing.model:
Two options for the print run.

Vidal is about 15% more expensive, but their lead time is four weeks against Orsan's eight. Orsan is the cheaper unit price by roughly 2,400 across the run.

Given that the launch date is fixed, I'd recommend Vidal. Orsan's eight weeks takes us past the launch, so the saving disappears the moment we have to air-freight or delay.

Happy to get both quotes in writing if you'd like them side by side.

conditionals.title: Negotiate with conditions
conditionals.brief: You want a week's extension on a report. You can offer something in return: you could deliver the executive summary on the original date so the client has something.
conditionals.task: Write to your manager using conditional language. Make the trade explicit.
include: A first conditional for what is genuinely possible
What you will deliver on the original date
What the extra week buys them

checks.label: Names what the extra time produces

selfCheck: Is the trade obvious in one read?
Did I avoid 'will' after 'if'?
Have I made saying yes easy?
conditionals.model:
If we can move the deadline to the 21st, I'll be able to include the client's revised Q4 figures, which is what the board will ask about.

In the meantime, if it helps, I can still deliver the executive summary on Friday as planned, so nobody is waiting on us.

If the 21st doesn't work, I'll send what I have on Friday and flag the figures as provisional. Let me know which you'd prefer.

tenses-at-work.title: Write the weekly update
tenses-at-work.brief: It's Friday. This week you finished the supplier report on Tuesday. Now you are writing a new guide for customers. Every Monday you have a team meeting at nine.
tenses-at-work.task: Write a short update for your team. Use the right tense for each thing: finished, happening now, and a habit.
include: What you finished, and when (past simple)
What you are doing now (present continuous)

checks.label: Uses the past simple for the finished report
Uses the present continuous for now
Avoids 'have finished' with a day
none: have finished the supplier report on tuesday

selfCheck: Is it clear what is finished and what is not?
Did I use the past simple with 'on Tuesday'?
tenses-at-work.model:
Hi team,

Here is my update. I finished the supplier report on Tuesday and sent it to Elena.

At the moment, I'm writing the new guide for customers. It will be ready next week.

See you at our team meeting on Monday. We always start at nine.

Ana

future-forms.title: Write about next month
future-forms.brief: Three things: your team is going to move to a new office in May (it's decided). You're meeting the new manager on Tuesday at 10 (it's in your calendar). You think the move will be good.
future-forms.task: Write a short message to your team about the three things. Use a different future form for each one.
include: The meeting with the present continuous ('I'm meeting…')

checks.label: Uses the present continuous for the meeting

selfCheck: Did I use three different future forms?
Is the day and time of the meeting clear?
future-forms.model:
Hi everyone,

Some news: we're going to move to the new office in May.

I'm meeting the new manager on Tuesday at 10 a.m. to talk about the move. I'll tell you everything after the meeting.

I think the new office will be great!

Ana

present-perfect.title: Write the status report
present-perfect.brief: You have spoken to the supplier and updated the timeline. You have not heard back about pricing, and you have been chasing it since Monday. The pilot has been running for six weeks and has already produced three issues.
present-perfect.task: Write the status update. This is what the present perfect is for.
include: What is done, without saying exactly when
How long something has been running

checks.label: Uses 'yet' or 'still' for what is missing
Avoids present perfect with a finished time

selfCheck: Is it clear what is outstanding?
Did I use 'for' with the length of time?
Would my manager know what to chase?
present-perfect.model:
Where we are on Northbridge.

I've spoken to the supplier and I've updated the timeline to reflect the new lead times. We still haven't heard back on the revised pricing, and I've been chasing that since Monday — I'll escalate to their account manager if there's nothing by Thursday.

The pilot has been running for six weeks now and has already surfaced three issues, all of them fixable. Nothing there changes the launch date.

modals.title: Write the advice note
modals.brief: A colleague is about to send a contract variation to a client without legal review. You think they should copy Legal, the client might ask for a discount, and the signed version genuinely has to be in before the 30th.
modals.task: Write them a short note covering all three: advice, possibility, and obligation.

checks.label: Gives advice with a soft modal
Marks the discount as a possibility

selfCheck: Can they tell advice from obligation?
Did I avoid sounding like their boss?
Is the deadline unmissable?
modals.model:
Before that goes out, I think you should copy Legal in — variations on this contract have bitten us before, and it only costs a day.

The client might come back asking for a discount on the extended term, so it's worth having a number in mind before they do.

One hard point: the signed version has to be with us before the 30th, otherwise the current rates lapse and we start again.

workplace-vocabulary.title: Fix the weak sentences
workplace-vocabulary.brief: This is from a colleague's CV: 'I did a project for the company. I made the process better. My responsible was happy.'
workplace-vocabulary.task: Rewrite it. Use better verbs, fix the false friend, and add a number.
include: A better verb than 'made better' (for example 'improved')
selfCheck: Did I change 'did' and 'made'?
Is there a number?
workplace-vocabulary.model: I managed a project for the sales team. I improved the order process and reduced the time for each order by 20%. My manager was very happy with the results, and she asked me to lead the next project.

describing-data.title: Describe the chart (IELTS Task 1 style)
describing-data.brief: A chart shows two lines over six months. Online sales rise from 100k in January to 280k in June, with the steepest rise between March and April. In-store sales stay flat at around 150k throughout.
describing-data.task: Describe what the chart shows. Open with one sentence of overview, then give the detail. Do not give your opinion.
include: An overview sentence before any detail
A proportion, not just raw numbers
describing-data.minWordsLabel: At least 100 words (IELTS Task 1 minimum is 150)

checks.label: Uses 'by' or 'to' correctly with a figure

selfCheck: Did I open with an overview before any numbers?
Did I compare rather than list?
Did I keep my opinion out of it?
describing-data.model:
Overall, online sales rose sharply across the six-month period while in-store sales remained flat, so the gap between the two channels widened considerably.

Online sales began at 100,000 in January and climbed steadily to 280,000 by June, almost tripling over the period. The steepest rise came between March and April, when the figure jumped by roughly 60,000 in a single month. After April, growth continued, but at a slower pace.

In-store sales, by contrast, stayed close to 150,000 throughout, with only minor fluctuations from month to month. By June, online sales were almost twice as high as in-store sales, a substantial margin for a channel that had started the period a third lower.

linking-expressions.title: Write the short argument
linking-expressions.brief: Your company is deciding whether to keep the central office or move fully remote.
linking-expressions.task: Write a short argued paragraph. Give one point in favour, one against, and a conclusion, joined properly.
selfCheck: Does each linker do a different job?
Are there three or fewer linkers?
Did I reach an actual conclusion?
linking-expressions.model:
Moving fully remote would cut our fixed costs significantly, and it would widen the pool of people we can hire. Moreover, the last two years suggest that delivery has not suffered.

However, the informal learning that junior staff get from sitting near senior colleagues is very hard to reproduce online. For example, our two most recent leavers both cited isolation rather than pay.

Overall, I'd argue for a hybrid model: keep a smaller central office for two days a week, and let the rest be flexible.

report-writing.title: Write the recommendation report
report-writing.brief: Two supplier options. B is 12% more expensive but delivers in half the time and has a better fault record. Transition cost is estimated at 8 to 10k in the first quarter.
report-writing.task: Write the opening of the report. State the recommendation first, then the scope, the evidence and the risk.
include: The recommendation, in the first sentence
The main risk, named by you

checks.label: Names the risk with a figure
Avoids building suspense
none: in this report i will talk about

selfCheck: Is my conclusion in the first sentence?
Did I name the risk before someone else did?
Could a busy reader stop after the first paragraph and still know what to do?
report-writing.model:
We recommend moving to Supplier B from the next contract period.

This report compares the two shortlisted suppliers on cost, lead time and reliability. Supplier B is 12% more expensive per unit, but delivers in half the time and has a materially better fault record over the last three years.

The main risk is transition cost, which we estimate at 8 to 10k in the first quarter, largely in re-tooling and staff time. Our view is that this is recovered within two quarters through reduced expediting costs. Detail is in sections 3 and 4.

passive-reported.title: Write the incident report
passive-reported.brief: On 14 March the payment system was unavailable for 3 hours 20 minutes. About 2,400 transactions failed. The cause was a configuration change deployed without the staging check. All transactions have since been reprocessed and customers notified.
passive-reported.task: Write the factual section and one recommendation. Keep individuals' names out of the factual section.
include: One recommendation with an owner and a date

checks.label: Uses the passive for the facts
Names no individual in the facts
Recommendation has an owner or a date

selfCheck: Would a regulator find this factual and neutral?
Did I switch to the active voice for the recommendation?
Is the fix specific enough to be checked later?
passive-reported.model:
On 14 March the payment system was unavailable for 3 hours 20 minutes, from 09:14 to 12:34.

Approximately 2,400 transactions failed during this period and were not automatically retried. All affected transactions have since been reprocessed and the customers concerned have been notified.

The outage was caused by a configuration change deployed at 09:10 without the required staging check.

We recommend that the staging check is made a mandatory gate in the deployment pipeline, owned by the platform team, by 30 April.

interview-language.title: Answer the interview question
interview-language.brief: You are in a job interview. The interviewer says: 'Tell me about a project you're proud of, and what you'd do differently.'
interview-language.task: Answer out loud. Situation, what you did, the result, and one honest thing you would change.
checklist: I described a specific project, not a general skill
I said what I personally did, not just what the team did
I gave a result with a number
I named one real thing I would change
I used past simple for the finished project
I finished on the lesson rather than trailing off
interview-language.model:
The one I'd pick is the checkout rebuild we did last year. The problem was that we were losing about a third of users at the payment step, and nobody could say why.

I ran the discovery phase, which meant sitting with support for two days and going through recorded sessions. We found that the card form was rejecting valid postcodes. We tested three versions over six weeks, and the one we shipped brought drop-off down from 33% to 12%. That's roughly 400,000 a year in recovered revenue.

What I'd do differently is involve the support team at the start rather than at the design review. They spotted two failure cases in ten minutes that we'd missed in three weeks, and that cost us about ten days. Since then I bring support into discovery on anything customer-facing.

speaking-structure.title: Speak for two minutes
speaking-structure.brief: You are asked in a meeting: 'Should we extend the deadline or ship what we have?'
speaking-structure.task: Give a structured answer. Announce how many reasons you have, give them, illustrate one with an example, and close.
checklist: I stated my position in the first sentence
I announced how many reasons I had
I actually gave that number of reasons
I used a real example
I signposted ('first', 'second', 'so overall')
I spoke for at least 90 seconds without a long pause
speaking-structure.model:
My view is that we should extend, and there are two reasons.

The first is data quality. The client's revised figures only arrived on Tuesday, and if we ship now, the report goes out with numbers we know are three weeks old. The second is cost of rework. A rushed version doesn't save time, it moves the time somewhere less visible.

For example, last quarter we shipped the Northbridge report on the original date and then spent three weeks correcting it, which cost more than the delay would have.

So overall, I'd take the extra week, tell the client today rather than on Friday, and send the executive summary on the original date so nobody is left waiting.

small-talk.title: Start and end a conversation
small-talk.brief: You are at a conference dinner. You sit next to someone from another company. You liked her talk this morning.
small-talk.task: Say hello, ask one question about her work, and end the conversation politely.
checklist: I said hello and my name
I said something nice about her talk
I asked a question about her work
I ended politely ('It was nice talking to you')
I asked to stay in contact (email or LinkedIn)
small-talk.model: Hi, I'm Ana. I work for Vidal in Madrid. I really liked your talk this morning, especially the part about prices. Do you work with customers in Spain too? … Oh, that's interesting. Well, it was nice talking to you. Can I send you an email next week? Enjoy your dinner!

ielts-speaking.title: IELTS Speaking: listen, then answer
ielts-speaking.brief: IELTS SKILL. Part 3 rewards developed, non-memorised opinion. The best preparation is listening to how fluent speakers structure an argument, then doing it yourself.
ielts-speaking.task: Choose one talk or episode on a work-related topic: automation, remote work, productivity, or the future of jobs. Watch or listen once without stopping, then once more with notes.

resources.label: TED Talks — search for 'future of work' or 'automation'

ielts-speaking.note: These open in a new tab. Nothing is tracked, and you can use any other source you prefer.
ielts-speaking.then: Answer this in writing, as if speaking: 'Do you think artificial intelligence will make most office jobs disappear in the next twenty years?' Take a position, give two reasons, use one point from what you listened to, and concede the other side.
include: One point taken from what you listened to

checks.label: Refers to what you listened to

selfCheck: Did I answer the actual question asked?
Would this sound rehearsed, or like thinking?
Did I develop each reason rather than listing them?
ielts-speaking.model:
I don't think they'll disappear, though I'd expect them to change substantially.

The main reason is that most office roles aren't a single task. They're a bundle of judgement, negotiation and relationship management, and only some of that is automatable. The speaker in the episode I listened to made a similar point about accountancy: software has done the arithmetic for thirty years, and there are more accountants now than there were, because the job moved towards advice.

Secondly, organisations adopt technology far more slowly than the technology arrives.

That said, I'd accept that roles which genuinely are one repetitive task are at real risk, and the transition could be painful even if the total number of jobs holds up. So my position would be significant disruption, but not disappearance.

ielts-reading.title: IELTS Reading: read, then summarise
ielts-reading.brief: IELTS SKILL. Academic Reading gives you three passages and 40 questions in 60 minutes, so reading quickly and accurately for the main idea matters more than understanding every word.
ielts-reading.task: Find one article of about 800 to 1,200 words on a work, technology or environment topic. Give yourself 10 minutes maximum. Skim for the structure first, then read for detail.

resources.label: BBC Learning English — News Review and features
TED Talks — transcripts are under each talk

ielts-reading.note: Time yourself. Ten minutes, then stop reading and write from memory and notes.
ielts-reading.then: Write a summary of the article in your own words. Then write one statement about it that would be TRUE, one that would be FALSE, and one that would be NOT GIVEN, and label each one.
include: A summary of the main argument
selfCheck: Is my NOT GIVEN genuinely absent from the text, rather than contradicted?
Did I paraphrase, or did I copy phrases?
Could I point to the exact line that proves my TRUE statement?
ielts-reading.model:
The article argues that hybrid working has become permanent for most large employers, but that it has created a new problem: junior staff learn far less informally than they used to. The writer suggests that mandating office days has not solved this, because attendance is not the same as contact.

TRUE — Most large employers have kept some form of hybrid working. (The text states a majority retained it.)

FALSE — The writer argues that office mandates have solved the training problem. (The text says the opposite: mandates have not solved it.)

NOT GIVEN — Hybrid working has reduced company profits. (The text discusses training and attendance, but never mentions profit, so this cannot be judged either way.)

linking-basics.title: Write about a problem
linking-basics.brief: The new laptops are late. The supplier had a problem. They arrive on Thursday, not Monday. The team can use the old laptops until Thursday.
linking-basics.task: Write a short email to your team. Say what the problem is, why, and what the team can do. Join your ideas with linking words.
include: The problem: the laptops are late

checks.label: Doesn't use 'because' and 'so' together
none: because the supplier had a problem, so
because the supplier has a problem, so

selfCheck: Does each linking word do a different job?
Are my sentences short and clear?
linking-basics.model:
Hi all,

The new laptops are late because the supplier had a problem. They arrive on Thursday, not Monday. It's not ideal, but you can use your old laptops until then, so please don't return them yet.

Thanks,
Ana

reading-strategies.title: Read a real article, then summarise it
reading-strategies.brief: At work you rarely read every word. You skim for the main point, scan for the details you need, and keep what the text says separate from what you think.
reading-strategies.task: Find a short work-related article or report in English (300 to 600 words). Give yourself five minutes. Skim the title and headings first, then scan for two details.

resources.label: BBC Learning English — News Review and features

reading-strategies.note: Five minutes of reading, then close the page and write from your notes.
reading-strategies.then: Write a short summary for a colleague who hasn't read it: the main point, two details, one thing the writer suggests, and one thing the text doesn't say.
include: The main point, with 'The main point is…'
One thing the writer suggests or implies
One thing the text doesn't say

checks.label: Reports a detail with a source phrase
Says what the text doesn't say

selfCheck: Did I keep my own opinion out of the summary?
Could a colleague understand the text from my summary alone?
reading-strategies.model: The main point of the article is that more companies are testing a four-day week, mainly to keep their staff. According to the article, most of the companies in a recent trial decided to continue, and sick days fell sharply. The writer suggests that smaller companies find the change easier than large ones. However, the article doesn't say what happened to customer satisfaction, which is what my manager would want to know.

linking-formal.title: Write the recommendation email
linking-formal.brief: Your company must choose between two logistics partners. Rapido is 8% cheaper, but only 91% of its deliveries were on time last year. Transol costs more, but 98% of its deliveries were on time, and it will hold its prices for two years if you sign by June. Last year, late deliveries cost you two major clients.
linking-formal.task: Write a short, formal email to your director recommending one partner. Use formal linkers to compare, concede, set a condition and reason from a known fact.
include: A condition ('provided that' or 'as long as')
A known fact to reason from ('given that' or 'in light of')

checks.label: Doesn't double up 'although' and 'but'
none: although transol is more expensive, but

selfCheck: If I replace each linker with its meaning, does the sentence still make sense?
Is the recommendation in the first or last sentence, where the director will see it?
linking-formal.model:
Dear Andrea,

I recommend that we appoint Transol as our logistics partner.

Rapido's rates are around 8% lower, whereas Transol's are higher on every route. Nevertheless, Transol delivered 98% of orders on time last year, while Rapido managed only 91%. Given that late deliveries cost us two major clients last year, I believe reliability should carry more weight than price in this decision.

Transol has also agreed to hold its prices for two years, provided that we sign the contract by the end of June. Consequently, the cost gap would narrow over the life of the contract.

I would be happy to discuss this before the board meeting.

Kind regards,
Samuel
